podcast.title: Advocacy for Women's Liberation
podcast.body: Bobby Gentry explicitly stated that her song "Fancy" was her "strongest statement for women's lib," expressing her agreement with the movement and its core issues such as equality, equal pay, daycare centers, and abortion rights. This was a powerful stance for a woman in 1970. "Gentry said, Fancy is my strongest statement for women's lib if you really listen to it."

podcast.title: Diverse Talents
podcast.body: Beyond her songwriting and singing, Bobby Gentry was a DJ for Armed Forces Radio and is believed to have painted the portraits for her album covers, including "Fancy" and "Patchwork." "According to Tara Murtha who wrote an excellent book on Gentry in Ode de Billy Joe for the 33 in a third book series, Gentry was a DJ for Armed Forces Radio and she probably painted the portraits for the album covers for fancy and patchwork."

podcast.title: Early Life and Musical Education
podcast.body: Bobby Gentry hailed from Mississippi but was not the "hillbilly" stereotype the industry tried to impose on her. She studied music in California from the age of 13. "And even though she was from Mississippi, she was not the hillbilly that the industry tried to make her into. She had studied music in California starting at the age of 13."

podcast.title: Las Vegas Residency (1960s-1970s)
podcast.body: For ten years, Bobby Gentry starred in critically acclaimed shows in Las Vegas. These performances were known for their over-the-top set designs, outrageous costumes often designed by Gentry herself, and stellar choreography, including a "gender-bending tribute to Elvis Presley" where she performed in a skin-tight, glittering pantsuit. "In for 10 years, she starred in shows in Las Vegas that were... critically acclaimed for over-the-top set design, outrageous costumes she often designed herself in stellar choreography, including a gender-bending tribute to Elvis Presley performed in a skin-tight, glittering pantsuit."

podcast.title: Retirement from Music (Late 1970s)
podcast.body: Bobby Gentry abruptly walked away from her music career by the end of the 1970s. Her last known public appearance was on the Christmas episode of Johnny Carson's show in 1978, after which she ceased performing, giving interviews, or participating in retrospectives. "She was on the Christmas episode of Johnny Carson's show in 1978 and that was it. No more performing, no more interviews, no retrospectives, nothing. She just walked away."
